newsitem.title: USA: U.S. calls Burma's visa ban "ludicrous".
newsitem.headline: U.S. calls Burma's visa ban "ludicrous".

text.p: The United States dismissed as "ludicrous" a Burmese clampdown on Friday on entry visas for U.S. citizens and said it was "not going to matter one bit" to anyone in the U.S. government.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns charged that Burmese military authorities had "made fools of themselves" by their allegations against the United States.

Rangoon imposed the visa restrictions in response to an American ban, announced on Thursday by U.S. President Bill Clinton, on travel by Burmese government leaders and their families to the United States.

"This is really ludicrous," Burns said. "This is a desperate attempt by the military dictators in Burma to try to do something to divert attention of their own people from the real problem which exists in the Burmese government," he told a news briefing.

"I can assure you that is not going to matter one bit to any of us in Washington, D.C. who make policy or implement it or talk about it, that we can't travel to Rangoon at this time," Burns told a news briefing.

The complicated restrictions issued by Burma did not make clear exactly which U.S. citizens would be banned, but Burns said they mirrored the U.S. measures by debarring visas to U.S. government officials and their immediate families. Diplomats are not affected in either case.
Clinton's proclamation followed U.S. outrage over the Burmese military government's arrest of hundreds of pro-democracy activists over the last week.

Washington has also been incensed by Burmese charges that charge d'affaires in Rangoon Marilyn Meyers interfered in the country's internal affairs by statements warning of adverse U.S. reaction to Burma's crackdown on dissent.

Burns said the charges "would almost be comical if it wasn't so serious. These people have made fools of themselves by the allegations that they've hurled against the United States -- the military dictators."
Meyers left Burma on Friday at the end of her posting. Burns said her successor, Kent Wiedemann, would arrive there in about 10 days' time.
"We expect that Mr. Wiedemann will be well treated, and that he will not be subjected to these scurrilous attacks," the U.S. spokesman said.
